title: Bunyan's Pilgrim, in Xhosa
hook: Ordained in Glasgow, he carried one book home. *He gave it to his people in Xhosa.*
dateline: Tiyo Soga · This week, on November 21, 1866 · Mgwali, Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: On November 21, 1866, Tiyo Soga finished translating the first part of Pilgrim's Progress into Xhosa.

lead_image.alt: Photograph of Tiyo Soga, seated, a book in his hand
lead_image.credit: Tiyo Soga, frontispiece photograph, John A. Chalmers, *Tiyo Soga: A Page of South African Mission Work* (1877) · Public domain, via Internet Archive

story: A quarter past nine at night. A Xhosa minister wrote one more line in his journal: “Finished, through the goodness of Almighty God, the translation of the first part of Pilgrim's Progress, my fingers aching with writing.” He was Tiyo Soga, and he wrote it 160 years ago this past Saturday, on November 21, 1866.

He was born in 1829 near the Tyume River in the Eastern Cape, a son of Jotello, a councillor to the Ngqika chief, and Nosuthu. He went to school at Lovedale, and when war shut it in 1846, its principal, William Govan, took him to Scotland. He was baptized in Glasgow in May 1848. Bunyan's story of a pilgrim walking toward the Celestial City was his “constant companion” through his studies; he translated “a large portion” of it, he later wrote, while still a student in Scotland.

On December 23, 1856, the United Presbyterian Presbytery of Glasgow ordained him, the first African minister ordained in Britain. On February 27, 1857, he married Janet Burnside, a Scot. When they landed at Algoa Bay that July, “black and white turned to stare at us” in the streets, he wrote. He wrote plainly about “the prejudices existing in the Colony against colour.”

He went home to a people in grief. In 1857 the Xhosa were starving after the cattle-killing, and that July he wrote a hymn in isiXhosa, “Lizalis' idinga lakho” (“Fulfil your promise”). At the Mgwali mission he preached, wrote hymns, and wore out his voice. In 1866 chronic laryngitis sent him away for six months.

Back at Mgwali that July, he went back to Bunyan. After the November night he finished, he sent the manuscript to the Free Church press at Lovedale and dedicated it to Govan, the man who had taken him to Scotland as a boy. “We publish only the first part of it,” he told a friend, “and it is all that is finished.” U-Hambo lom-Hambi “was read with avidity at every station,” his biographer wrote, and missionaries read it aloud at services. Britannica compares its influence on the Xhosa language to the King James Bible's on English. Lovedale was printing a third edition by 1889.

Soga knew what his sons would face. In a notebook he called The Inheritance of My Children, he told them never to be ashamed of their father's people and to take their place as Africans, not as Englishmen. Among its numbered maxims: “Insult no human being; but fear no man when you are in the right.”

He would wait, he said, to see how the first part was received. Worn down by illness, by most accounts tuberculosis, he died at the Tutura mission (his biographer spells it Tutuka) on August 12, 1871, aged about 42, his mother Nosuthu beside him. A fellow missionary asked whether the Saviour was precious to him. He whispered, “Yes!”
Bunyan's pilgrim ends his journey at a river with the city in sight. Tiyo Soga reached his early. The book he finished that November night kept walking without him, in his own people's words.

quote.text: Finished, through the goodness of Almighty God, the translation of the first part of Pilgrim's Progress, my fingers aching with writing.
quote.source: Tiyo Soga, journal, 21 November 1866, quoted in John A. Chalmers, Tiyo Soga: A Page of South African Mission Work (1877), ch. XVIII, c. p. 340

scripture.text: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
scripture.note: Pilgrims who died before they saw what they hoped for.

why: Tiyo Soga's Xhosa Pilgrim's Progress, U-Hambo lom-Hambi, helped shape written isiXhosa and is still reprinted; his hymns are still sung in South African churches. God used a man doubted on both sides of the colour line to give his people a pilgrim who spoke their language.
prompt: What story of faith could I put into words someone near me understands?
ask_yourself: What story of faith could I put into words someone near me understands?
why_reel_line: God gave the Xhosa a pilgrim who spoke their language, through a man both sides doubted.
